newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada lumber exports to U.S. to stay high - study.
newsitem.headline: Canada lumber exports to U.S. to stay high - study.

text.p: Canadian lumber exports to the United States will likely remain near last year's record pace in 1997 despite a new quota agreement between the two countries, a leading timber economist said on Tuesday.
Doug Smyth, research director for the IWA-Canada union, has just completed an in-depth study of the North American lumber market.

The report will be released in the next few weeks but he said in an interview today that it concluded Canada's 1997 shipments to the United States would be "about the same" as 1996's record 17.8 billion board feet.
"Obviously the quota has not restricted anything. That's primarily because of the U.S. timber supply. They simply can't supply their own needs," he said.

That should keep lumber prices firm, he said. While U.S. demand may be slightly softer this year, U.S. lumber producers resorted to temporary sources of supply in 1996 and these will not be available this year, Smyth said.
A five-year lumber trade agreement was reached by the United States and Canada little more than a year ago. It imposes duties on Canada's exports of more than 14.7 billion board feet.

But strong demand from the United States has prompted shippers to continue exporting lumber above that level and pay the duty. Many lumber analysts had expected the trade agreement to cause Canadian exports to decline.
